Introduction to cloud computing: IaaS, PaaS, and
SaaS
The rise of DevOps is inextricably linked to the rise of cloud computing. The cloud provides
the on-demand, programmable, and scalable idx_1542e611 infrastructure that makes many DevOps
practices, such as automation and IaC, not just possible but practical. Before the cloud, getting
a new server for a project could take weeks or months of procurement, racking, and
configuration. Today, you can provision a fleet of servers in minutes with a few clicks or lines of
code. In this section, we will define cloud computing and explore its fundamental service
models: IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.
What is cloud computing?
At its simplest, cloud idx_c96a7de1 computing is the on-demand delivery of IT resources over the internet
with pay-as-you-go pricing. Instead of buying, owning, and maintaining your own physical
data centers and servers, you can access technology services, such as computing power,
storage, and databases, from a cloud provider such as Amazon Web Services (AWS),
Microsoft Azure, or idx_3fede885 Google Cloud.
This model idx_d0376d38 offers several key advantages over traditional on-premises infrastructure:
Agility: The cloud allows idx_2ce0727f you to access resources in minutes, enabling you to innovate
and experiment much faster.
Elasticity: You can scale your resources up or down to instantly meet changing
business demand. You don't have to over-provision servers for peak loads that may
only occur a few times a year.
Cost savings: The cloud allows you to trade capital expense (buying hardware) for
variable expense (paying only for what you use).
Global reach: You can easily deploy your application in multiple geographic regions
around the world with just a few clicks, providing lower latency and a better experience
for your users.
To fully understand how these advantages are delivered, it's important to look at the different
cloud service models and how responsibility for managing resources is shared between you
and the provider.

Chapter 1 22
The service models: A shared responsibility
Cloud idx_ecd1c054 computing services are typically categorized into three main models: Infrastructure as
a Service (IaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), and Software as a Service (SaaS). These
models can be thought of as different layers of a technology stack, where each model abstracts
away a certain level of management responsibility from you and handles it for you. A popular
way to explain these models is through the pizza analogy:
Figure 1.2: "Pizza as a Service" analogy illustrating the differences between on-premises, IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
The diagram idx_c8d0a19f illustrates how responsibilities shift depending on the service. Now, let's look at
each of the models in a bit more depth.
23 Understanding the DevOps and Cloud Landscape
Infrastructure as a Service
IaaS is the most basic category of cloud computing services. With IaaS, a cloud provider hosts
idx_0683d052 the fundamental infrastructure components on your behalf – servers, storage, and networking
– in their data center. You access these resources over the internet and are responsible for
managing everything on top of them, including the operating system, middleware, data, and
applications.
IaaS gives you the maximum flexibility and management control over your IT resources,
making it the most similar to idx_20cea0ee traditional on-premises IT. It's like buying a pre-made pizza base,
cheese, and toppings from the store. You still have to assemble the pizza, bake it in your own
oven, and serve it at your own table, but you didn't have to make the dough or the sauce from
scratch.
When to use IaaS:
When you have legacy applications that you want to lift-and-shift to the cloud without
significant re-architecting
When you need complete control over the operating system and underlying
infrastructure
For idx_90fbdcc6 start-ups and idx_dbe57906 small companies that want to avoid the capital expense of buying
hardware
Examples: Amazon EC2, Azure Virtual Machines, Google Compute Engine.
Platform as a Service
PaaS provides a higher level of abstraction. With PaaS, the cloud provider manages not only the
idx_afaf8b56 underlying infrastructure (servers, storage, networking) but also the operating system,
middleware, and runtime environment. This frees idx_125c5c51 you to focus exclusively on developing and
managing your application code, without worrying about the underlying platform.
PaaS is designed to make it easier for developers to quickly create web or mobile apps, without
the complexity of setting up and managing the infrastructure. It's like ordering a pizza for
delivery. The pizza place takes care of making the pizza and baking it in their oven. All you have
to do is provide a table and drinks, and enjoy it when it arrives.
When to use PaaS:

When you idx_5500d2f0 want to accelerate the development of web and mobile applications
To support the entire application lifecycle (building, testing, deploying, managing, and
updating) in an integrated environment
When you want to enable developers to focus on writing code without being burdened
by infrastructure management

Chapter 1 24
Examples: AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Azure App Service, Google App Engine, Heroku.
Software as a Service
SaaS is idx_2ab9b265 the most comprehensive cloud service model. With SaaS, the cloud provider delivers a
complete, ready-to-use software application over the internet, typically on a subscription
basis. The provider manages everything: the infrastructure, the platform, and the application
software itself. You simply access the software through a idx_e25a05b9 web browser or mobile app.
SaaS is the most common cloud service model for end users. It's like going out to a restaurant
for pizza. You don't have to worry about anything except showing up and eating. The
restaurant handles the ingredients, the oven, the table, the drinks, and even the cleanup.
When to use SaaS:
For idx_1405eb91 common business applications idx_5cf98ea4 such as email, customer relationship
management (CRM), and enterprise resource planning (ERP)
When you want to provide idx_fdf58345 your employees with access to sophisticated applications
without the need for installation or maintenance
For applications where the demand is sporadic and a pay-as-you-go model is more
cost-effective
Examples: Google Workspace (Gmail, Google Docs), Microsoft 365, Salesforce, Dropbox, Slack.
Understanding idx_3165f95d these service models is crucial for making informed decisions about your cloud
strategy. As a DevOps professional, you will primarily work in the IaaS and PaaS space, using
these services as the building blocks for creating automated and scalable systems.
Now that we've explored the core service models and how responsibility shifts across them, the
next step is to look at the major cloud providers that deliver these services at scale.
Major cloud players: AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud
While there idx_3cd5c670 are many cloud providers in the market, the industry is dominated by three major
players, often referred to as the "big three" hyperscalers: Amazon Web Services (AWS),
Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP). Each of these providers offers a vast
portfolio of idx_4047d058 services, from basic compute and storage to advanced machine idx_ea859076 learning and
quantum computing. As a DevOps professional, you will almost certainly work with at least
one, and often more than one, of these platforms. This section provides a brief overview of each
of the major players.
•
•

25 Understanding the DevOps and Cloud Landscape
Amazon Web Services
AWS is the oldest and most dominant player in the cloud idx_5c362714 market. Launched in 2006, AWS
pioneered the IaaS model with the release of its Simple Storage Service (S3) and Elastic
Compute Cloud (EC2). By idx_d3821540 being the first to idx_44ca452d market, AWS has built a significant lead in market
share and has the most extensive global infrastructure.

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 1 24
chunks.content:
AWS is known for the sheer breadth and depth of its service offerings. It has a service for nearly
every conceivable use case, from traditional web hosting to satellite ground stations. This vast
portfolio makes it a popular choice for a wide range of customers, from start-ups to large
enterprises and government agencies. The AWS ecosystem is also incredibly mature, with a
massive community, extensive documentation, and a large marketplace of third-party tools
and services.
Key strengths:
Market leadership: The idx_d0aea7a0 largest market share and the most mature platform
Breadth of services: The most extensive portfolio of services and features
Global reach: The largest global network of data centers
Strong community: A massive and active community of users and experts
For a DevOps professional, AWS offers a rich set of tools specifically designed for building CI/
CD pipelines, such as AWS CodePipeline, AWS CodeBuild, and AWS CodeDeploy, which we
will explore in a later chapter.
Microsoft Azure
Microsoft Azure is the second-largest cloud idx_9ba01a66 provider and is the fastest-growing of the big
three. Launched in 2010, Azure has leveraged Microsoft's long-standing dominance in the
enterprise software market to idx_b1f23330 become a formidable competitor to AWS. Azure's key strength
lies in its deep integration with Microsoft's existing ecosystem of products, such as Windows
Server, Office 365, and Active Directory.
This makes Azure a natural choice for large enterprises that have already invested heavily in
Microsoft technologies. Azure also offers excellent support for hybrid cloud scenarios, allowing
organizations to seamlessly integrate their on-premises data centers with the Azure cloud. Its
PaaS offerings, such idx_adb3ab1e as Azure App Service, are highly regarded for their ease of use and
developer productivity.
Key strengths:
Enterprise focus: Strong appeal to large enterprises, especially those already using
Microsoft products.

Google Cloud Platform
GCP is the third-largest cloud provider. While it entered the market later than its main
competitors, GCP has differentiated idx_2e474e95 itself through its deep expertise in areas where Google
itself is a world leader: data analytics, machine learning, networking, and containerization.
Google is the original creator of idx_0231fe35 Kubernetes, the open source container orchestration platform
that has become the de facto standard for managing modern cloud-native applications. As a
result, GCP's managed Kubernetes offering, Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), is widely
idx_923b6c0f considered to be the most advanced and mature on the market. GCP is also highly respected for
its prowess in big data and AI, with services such as BigQuery and TensorFlow. It has built a
reputation for having a high-performance, secure, and cost-effective infrastructure, often
appealing to tech-savvy and data-driven companies.
Key strengths:
Expertise in containers: Leadership idx_ac8a7c9c in Kubernetes and container orchestration
Data and AI leadership: Cutting-edge services for big data analytics and machine
learning
High-performance networking: A fast and reliable global network
Open source commitment: A strong commitment to open source technologies
While each of these cloud providers has its own unique strengths and areas of focus, the reality
is that they are all converging. They all offer a core set of services for compute, storage,
networking, and databases, and they are all rapidly innovating and releasing new features. As a
DevOps professional, having familiarity with the core concepts and services of all three major
clouds will make you a more versatile and valuable asset in the modern technology landscape.

27 Understanding the DevOps and Cloud Landscape
Summary
In this chapter, we laid the foundational groundwork for your entire journey into DevOps and
the cloud. You learned that DevOps is far more than just tools; it is a cultural philosophy built
on collaboration, shared ownership, and continuous improvement, designed to break down
the "wall of confusion" between Development and Operations. We traced its origins,
understanding how the limitations of the Waterfall model gave rise to the Agile movement,

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 1 26
chunks.content:
and how DevOps evolved as the solution to Agile's "last mile problem" of delivery and
operations.
You now have a clear map of the DevOps lifecycle, seeing how an idea flows through the
continuous loop of planning, coding, building, testing, releasing, deploying, operating, and
monitoring. We established the critical technical principles of automation, continuous
integration, and continuous delivery that power this lifecycle.
Furthermore, you were introduced to the world of cloud computing, understanding the IaaS,
PaaS, and SaaS service models and meeting the three major players: AWS, Azure, and GCP.
Grasping these core concepts is essential because it provides the "why" behind all the technical
practices and tools you are about to learn. This knowledge will enable you to think critically
about your own processes and make informed decisions as you build and manage modern
software systems.
With this strong theoretical foundation in place, it's time to roll up your sleeves and move from
concept to practice. In the next chapter, we will take the crucial first step of building your
professional toolkit by setting up your DevOps workstation. You will get hands-on with the
essential command-line tools, install Git for version control, and prepare your environment for
the exciting projects that lie ahead.

Setting Up Your DevOps

Welcome to the first hands-on chapter of your DevOps journey. In Chapter 1, we explored the
crucial concepts, history, and culture that define DevOps and the cloud. Now, it's time to roll
up our sleeves and build the environment where all the action will happen: your personal
DevOps workstation. A properly configured workstation is a professional's most important
asset. It is your command center for writing code, managing infrastructure, building pipelines,
and interacting with the cloud. A clean, powerful, and efficient setup will not only make you
more productive but will also make the learning process smoother and more enjoyable.
In this chapter, we will walk through the essential steps to transform your computer into a
fully-featured development environment. We will start with the absolute foundation, the
command line, and build up from there, installing and configuring the core tools used by
DevOps engineers every day. By the end of this chapter, you will have a complete, professional-
grade toolkit, ready to tackle the exciting projects and challenges that lie ahead.
In this chapter, we're going to cover the following main topics:
Essential command-line (Bash) basics for DevOps
Installing and configuring Git for version control
Setting up your code editor: VS Code for DevOps
Introduction to Docker: installing Docker Desktop
Creating your AWS/Azure/GCP free-tier account

Technical requirements
This chapter involves installing software on your computer. You will need a computer with a
modern operating system (Windows 10/11, macOS, or a popular Linux distribution such as
Ubuntu) and administrator privileges to install applications. You will also need a stable
internet connection for downloading software and signing up for cloud accounts. Specific
software requirements and download links will be provided within each relevant section.
Essential command-line (Bash) basics for DevOps
Before we install idx_348ca007 any fancy tools, we must first master the most idx_794a0250 fundamental tool of all: the
command-line interface (CLI). While modern graphical user interfaces (GUIs) are great for
many tasks, the command line remains the undisputed king of power, speed, and automation
in the world of DevOps. Nearly every server you interact with, every script you write, and every
automation tool you use will be controlled through the CLI. Learning how to navigate and
operate your computer through text-based commands is a non-negotiable skill. In this section,

chunks.heading: Chapter 1 28

we will cover the essential Bash commands that will form the foundation of your work.
Why the command line?
In an age of intuitive graphical interfaces, why do professionals still rely on a text-based
terminal? The answer idx_afd77963 lies in its power and efficiency for complex tasks. The CLI is inherently
scriptable, allowing you to combine commands to automate tasks, which is the very heart of
DevOps automation. It's also the primary way engineers connect to and manage remote
servers in the cloud using protocols such idx_bb8d3da4 as SSH (Secure Shell). Furthermore, command-line
interfaces are incredibly resource-efficient, a critical factor on servers where every megabyte of
memory counts. They often provide more advanced options and finer control than their
graphical counterparts, and they idx_3a4807ba enable a powerful concept called composability, where you
can "pipe" the output of one tool directly into the input of another, chaining them together to
perform complex operations.
Getting to your terminal
The program idx_7141b6e0 you use to interact with the command line is called a terminal emulator, or
simply a terminal. The idx_d3eff9a3 program that runs inside the terminal, interprets idx_b741b5ed your commands, and
executes them idx_04e56b3e is called the shell. The most common shell on Linux and macOS is Bash
(Bourne Again SHell), and it has become the de facto standard for DevOps work.
Here are a few common shells:
On macOS: You idx_98eaea60 can find the Terminal app in Applications/Utilities, or by searching
for "Terminal" in Spotlight.

On Linux: The terminal idx_a5ca9b3c is usually accessible from your applications menu or with a
keyboard shortcut (often Ctrl + Alt + T).
On Windows: While idx_50e4a212 many DevOps tools originated with the Bash shell, Windows has
its own powerful, modern command-line shell called PowerShell. To idx_ebdfc7d4 get the best
experience, we recommend installing Windows Terminal from the Microsoft Store. It's
a modern, tabbed application that can host PowerShell, the traditional Command
Prompt, and other command-line tools.
To get started, open the Microsoft Store, search for "Windows Terminal", and install it.
Once installed, you can open it to get a PowerShell prompt by default.
Next, let's dive into the essential commands.
Core commands for navigation and file manipulation
To navigate idx_ba631ab8 the filesystem, you'll constantly use three core commands:
pwd (print working directory): Use this to find out where you are at any moment.
ls (list): Use this to see what files and folders there are in your current location. You can
modify its behavior with flags; for instance, ls -l provides a detailed list, and ls -a
shows all files, including hidden ones.
cd (change directory): Use this to move around. You can move to a specific location
with cd /path/to/directory, go up one level with cd .. , or return to your home
directory with cd ~ or just cd.
Creating and deleting items is just as straightforward:
mkdir my-project: Creates a new directory
touch new-file.txt: Creates a new empty file
rm new-file.txt: Removes a file
rmdir my-project: Removes an empty directory
rm -r my-project: The recursive flag deletes a directory that contains files.
You will also frequently need to copy and move files: The cp source.txt destination.txt
command copies a file, while adding the -r flag cp -r my-project my-project-backup,
copies an entire directory. The mv command can either move a file to a new directory, mv my-
file.txt /path/to/other/dir/, or rename it mv old-name.txt new-name.txt.

33 Setting Up Your DevOps Workstation
Follow-along exercise: Creating a project structure
Theory is good, but practice is better. Let's use the commands we've just learned about to
create a idx_1013ffef standard directory structure for a new web application project. This exercise will
simulate a common first step in any new development task.
First, open your terminal. Let's create a dedicated directory for all your projects from
this book. We'll put it in your home directory.
cd ~
mkdir devops-book-projects
Now, move into your new projects directory. This will be the starting point for all our
work.
cd devops-book-projects
Inside, let's create a directory for our first project, a simple website.
mkdir my-first-website
Navigate into the new project directory.

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 2 32
chunks.content:
cd my-first-website
Every good project needs a clear structure. Let's create two subdirectories: one for our
source code (src) and one for documentation (docs).
mkdir src docs
The rm command is powerful idx_510cef81 and permanent. There is no "Recycle Bin" on the
command line. Using rm -r (recursive) will delete a directory and everything inside it.
Adding the -f (force) flag, as in rm -rf /some/directory, will remove everything
without any confirmation prompts. Be extremely careful with this command, as a
mistake can wipe out important data. Double-check your pwd and the path you provide
to rm before pressing Enter.
Note

Use the ls command to verify that your directories were created.
ls
You should see docs src printed on your screen.
Now, let's create some empty files that you would typically find in a project like this.
We'll create an HTML file and a JavaScript file inside the src directory, and a README.md
file in the main project directory.
touch src/index.html
touch src/app.js
touch README.md
Let's add idx_f091fc29 a simple title to our README.md file. We can use the echo command, which
prints text, and the > redirection operator, which sends the output of a command into a
file (overwriting it if it exists).
echo "# My First Website Project" > README.md
To view the contents of the file and confirm our change, we can use the cat
(concatenate) command.
cat README.md
You should see # My First Website Project printed to the console.
Finally, let's check our work. Use the ls -lR command (-R means recursive, so it will
list the contents of subdirectories as well) to see the entire file structure you've created.
ls -lR
Congratulations! You have just used the command line to scaffold a new project, a task you will
perform countless times in your career. Take some time to practice these commands. Move
around, create files, and get comfortable in the terminal. It is your new professional home.
With a basic grasp of the command line, our next step is to install the single most important
tool in modern software development: Git.

Installing and configuring Git for version control
Git is a idx_9c8a9135 distributed version control system (VCS). It allows you idx_141af499 to track changes to your code
over time, collaborate idx_ce0c25da with other developers, and revert to previous versions if something goes
wrong. For a DevOps professional, understanding Git is not optional; it is a fundamental
requirement. Every piece of code, every configuration file, and every script you write should be
stored in a Git repository. Let's first look at its installation.
Installing Git on your system
Git is free, open source, and available for all major operating systems. The installation process
is straightforward.
Windows
The best idx_17d4f378 way to install Git on Windows is to idx_7d444f2c use Git for Windows. This package includes Git
itself, as well as a Bash emulation environment called Git Bash, which gives you a powerful
command-line experience.
Navigate to the official Git for Windows website: https://git-scm.com/download/
win.
Download the installer.
Run the installer.
You can safely accept the default options for most of the installation steps. The most important
choice is the default editor; if you plan to install VS Code as we recommend in the next section,
you can select Use Visual Studio Code as Git's default editor.
macOS
There are idx_d20683de several ways to install Git on macOS, but idx_9eea9d94 the easiest is to use the Homebrew package
manager. If you don't have Homebrew, you can install it by pasting the command from its
official site (https://brew.sh) into your terminal. Once Homebrew is installed, do the
following:
Open your terminal.
Run the following command to install Git:
brew install git
Alternatively, if you install Apple's Xcode Command Line Tools, they also include a version of
Git. You can install them by running xcode-select --install.

Chapter 2 36
Linux (Ubuntu/Debian)
On Debian-based idx_7628fab1 Linux distributions idx_9078dbde like Ubuntu, you can idx_350a78fb install Git using the apt package
idx_20511eaa manager.
Open your terminal.
First, update your package index:
sudo apt update
Then, install Git:
sudo apt install git
Once Git is installed on your system, the next step is to configure it so your commits are
properly identified and your workflow is set up for success.
First-time Git configuration
After installing Git, there are a few essential configuration steps you need to perform. These
settings are idx_6daa1a39 stored in a global configuration file and will be used for every Git repository on
your system. You only need to do this once.
Open your terminal (or Git Bash on Windows) and run the following two commands, replacing
the example name and email with your own.
Set your user name. This name will be attached to every commit you make.
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
Set your email address. This email will also be associated with your commits. It's best
practice to use the same email you plan to use for services such as GitHub or GitLab.
git config --global user.email "youremail@example.com"
These two settings are critical because they are how Git identifies who made which changes.
This is the foundation of collaborative development and accountability. You can verify your
settings by running git config --list and looking for the user.name and user.email
entries. With Git installed and configured, you now have the power to track the history of your
projects. In the next chapter, we will dive deep into how to use Git to manage your first project.

With Git installed idx_478e4390 and configured, the final piece of your development setup is idx_765f62fe a powerful code
editor. In the next section, we'll set up Visual Studio Code (VS Code), the preferred editor for

Setting up your code editor: VS Code for DevOps
Every craftsperson needs a good workshop, and for a developer or DevOps engineer, that
workshop idx_6960b560 is the code editor. While you can write code in a simple text editor, a modern code
editor provides powerful features that dramatically improve productivity, such as syntax
highlighting, code completion, debugging tools, and an integrated terminal. While there are
many excellent editors available, the industry standard and our recommendation for this book
is VS Code.
Why Visual Studio Code?
VS Code, developed by Microsoft, is a free, open source, and cross-platform code editor that
has taken idx_e2272f78 the development world by storm. Its popularity is due to a combination of factors
that make it particularly well-suited for DevOps work. It is incredibly lightweight and fast, yet
boasts a massive marketplace of extensions for adding new languages and tools, allowing you
to customize it perfectly for your needs. Crucially for DevOps, it features a built-in terminal, so
you can run tools such as Git and Docker without leaving the editor. It also has best-in-class
Git integration for managing your code changes and is supported by a huge community
creating tutorials and providing support.
Installing and touring VS Code
Installing idx_a5f711a9 VS Code is as simple as visiting the official idx_be751676 website, downloading the version for your
operating system, and running the installer:
Navigate idx_84d1b8dd to the official VS Code website: https://code.visualstudio.com/.
The website should automatically detect your OS and recommend the correct
download. Click the Download button.
Run the installer. On Windows and macOS, you can accept the default options. On
Windows, ensure the Add to PATH option is checked during installation, as this will
allow you to open VS Code from the command line.

With VS idx_33ef7517 Code installed and ready to use, you can idx_dc26a47c enhance its capabilities even further by
adding extensions tailored for DevOps workflows.
Essential extensions for a DevOps workstation
The true power of VS Code lies in its extensions. Let's install a few that are essential for the
topics idx_df6579d7 we'll be covering in this book. Go to the Extensions view (the icon with the four squares

core dockerd daemon that manages containers), the Docker CLI client (the docker command

Chapter 2 52
3
Mastering Version Control with
Git and GitHub
In the last chapter, you assembled your professional DevOps toolkit. You now have a powerful
command line, a feature-rich code editor, and access to the cloud. With your workstation
ready, we can now learn how to use the most critical tool in that toolkit: Git. If the command
line is how you talk to your systems, Git is how you remember, organize, and share their
stories. It is the bedrock of modern software development, enabling collaboration, ensuring
quality, and providing a safety net for every line of code you write.
This chapter will take you from zero to hero with version control. We will start with the
absolute fundamentals: how Git thinks and the core commands you'll use every day. From
there, we will explore powerful branching strategies that allow teams to work in parallel
without chaos. We will then put it all into practice with a hands-on project, using GitHub, the
world's largest platform for hosting Git repositories, to simulate a real-world team workflow.
You will learn the art of the pull request, the importance of code reviews, and how to navigate
the inevitable merge conflict. By the end of this chapter, you will not just know Git commands;
you will understand the workflow that powers the world's most successful technology teams.
In this chapter, we're going to cover the following main topics:
Git fundamentals: Commits, pushes, and pulls
Branching for collaboration: The GitFlow strategy
Hands-on: Managing your first team project on GitHub
The power of pull requests and code reviews
Resolving merge conflicts
•
•
•
•
•
Technical requirements
For this chapter, you will need all the tools we installed and configured in Chapter 2.
Specifically, ensure you have Git installed and globally configured with your user name and
email. You will also need Visual Studio Code and a comfortable terminal. Finally, you will need
a free account on GitHub. If you don't have one yet, you can sign up at https://github.com/
join.
You can download the example project and code for this book by following the instructions in
the Download the example code files section in the Preface of this book.
This chapter's code files are included in the downloadable code bundle.
Git fundamentals: Commits, pushes, and pulls
Before we can build complex collaborative workflows, we must understand how Git operates
idx_8999322e at a fundamental level. Git is more than just a tool for saving files; it's a content-addressable
filesystem that thinks about your data like a series of snapshots. This is different from older
version control systems that thought about changes as a list of file-based differences (deltas).
This snapshot-based approach is what makes Git so fast and powerful. In this section, we will
explore the core concepts of a Git repository and the fundamental three-command workflow

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 2 52
chunks.content:
you will use constantly.
The three trees: Understanding Git's architecture
To use Git idx_88ed5ac5 effectively, you need to understand that it manages your project's state across three
main areas, often called the three trees. These aren't literal trees, but conceptual zones that your
files move between as you work. To understand how Git tracks changes, it helps to visualize its
three main areas: the working directory, the staging area, and the repository.

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 54
chunks.content:
Chapter 3 54
Figure 3.1: The Git workflow showing how files move between the working directory, staging area, and repository
using git add and git commit
As can idx_64bdf899 be seen from Figure 3.1, Git manages your project across three distinct areas, each
serving a specific purpose in the version control process:
Working Directory: This is your project folder on your computer's filesystem. It's the
tangible directory you can see and interact with, containing all the files and
subdirectories of your project. This is where you will actually edit your code, add new
files, and delete old ones. It is your live, unsaved sandbox.
Staging Area (or Index): This is one of Git's most powerful and sometimes confusing
features. The staging area is an intermediate zone. It's a file, generally contained in your
Git directory, that stores information about what will go into your next commit. It
allows you to carefully craft your next snapshot. You don't have to commit every single
change you've made in your working directory. Instead, you can selectively add (stage)
certain changes to the staging area and leave others out. This lets you build up a logical,
well-defined commit.
The Repository (or .git directory): This is where Git permanently stores your project's
history. When you make a commit, Git takes the files as they are in the staging area and
stores a snapshot of them forever in your local repository. This repository is contained
within a hidden .git directory at the root of your project. It contains all your commits,
branches, tags, and other metadata. This is the "database" of your project's history.
The fundamental local workflow in Git involves moving changes between these three trees.
You make modifications in the working directory, you use the git add command to move
those changes to the staging area, and you use the git commit command to permanently save
the snapshot from the staging area in the repository.
•
•
•
55 Mastering Version Control with Git and GitHub
Let's put this into practice.
Initializing your first repository
We'll use idx_92ab032b the my-first-website directory that we set up during the command-line exercise in

chunks.heading: Chapter 2. Navigate to that directory in your terminal.
chunks.content:
Chapter 2. Navigate to that directory in your terminal.
Go to your project directory.
cd ~/devops-book-projects/my-first-website
Now, to turn this regular directory into a Git repository, you use the git init
command:
git init
Git will respond with something like Initialized empty Git repository in /path/to/my-
first-website/.git/. You have now created the .git directory, and your project is officially
under version control.
The core workflow: Add, commit, and check status
Now that idx_de63b614 we have a repository, let's make our first commit. This follows a simple process.
Checking the status with git status
The git status command is your best friend. You will use it constantly to see the current state
idx_eb62d0c6 of your working directory and staging area. Run it now:
git status
Git will tell you that you are on the default branch and that you have untracked files. These
are the files we created in the last chapter (README.md, src/). Git sees them, but it isn't tracking
their history yet.
1.
2.

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 56
chunks.content:
Chapter 3 56
Staging changes with git add
To start tracking these files, we need to add them to the staging area. We do this with the git
add command. You can add files one by one, or you can add all changes in the current directory
idx_3cdbc347 and its subdirectories using a period (.). The staging area's real power shows when you want
to commit only part of your work. Imagine you've modified two files, index.html and
style.css, but only want to commit the HTML changes right now. You simply run git add
index.html to stage only that file, leaving style.css in your working directory as an
uncommitted change. This lets you build focused, logical commits instead of one large
"changed everything" snapshot.
git add .
Now, run git status again. You'll see that the files are now listed under Changes to be
committed. They have been moved from the working directory (conceptually) to the staging
area.
Saving snapshots with git commit
With our changes staged, we are ready to create our first permanent snapshot. We do this with
the git commit command. Every commit must have a commit message, which is a short
idx_fee6334d description of the changes you made. A good commit message is crucial for understanding the
project's history later on. You can provide a message directly on the command line using the -m
flag:
git commit -m "Initial commit: Add project structure and README"
main versus master: Clarifying the confusion
You may notice that older Git installations and documentation refer to the default
branch as master, while newer ones use main. In 2020, GitHub changed the default
branch name from master to main for all new repositories, and Git itself followed suit.
The two names are functionally identical; it's just a name, but main is now the modern
standard. Throughout this book, we use main, but if you ever encounter a repository
that uses master, simply substitute accordingly.
Note
57 Mastering Version Control with Git and GitHub
You've done it! You have created your first commit. Git will show you a summary of the
commit, including its unique ID (a hash) and the files that were changed. If you run git
status one more time, it will tell you that there is nothing to commit, working tree clean,
meaning your working directory, staging area, and the latest commit in your repository are all
in sync.
Working with remote repositories
So far, everything idx_a1f5526a we've done has been on our local machine. This is great for personal projects,
but the real power of Git comes from collaboration. To collaborate, we idx_96fd0506 use remote
repositories, which are versions of your project hosted on a server somewhere, typically on a
platform such as GitHub.
Pushing changes with git push
After you've made some commits locally, you will want to share them with your team. The git

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 56
chunks.content:
push command is used to upload your local commits to a remote repository. This updates idx_86e8142e the
remote repository with the changes you've made on your machine. Before pushing, two
commands will quickly become part of your daily routine. Run git diff to see a line-by-line
view of every unstaged change in your working directory. It shows exactly what has been
added (in green) or removed (in red) since your last commit. Run git log to browse the
commit history: it prints a reverse-chronological list of commits showing each commit's
unique hash, author, date, and message. Both commands help you review your own work
before sharing it.
Pulling Changes with git pull
Conversely, when your teammates have made changes and pushed them to the remote
repository, you will want to get those changes onto your local machine. The git pull
command idx_33c097c5 is used to fetch the latest changes from a remote repository and merge them into
your current local branch. It's how you stay up to date with the rest of the team. It's worth
knowing that git pull is actually two operations in one: it first runs git fetch to download
the remote changes into a temporary area, then automatically merges them into your branch. If
you want to inspect what changed before merging, you can run git fetch on its own; it
updates your remote-tracking references without touching your working branch, letting you
review with git log origin/main before committing to the merge. You may also encounter
the term rebase as an alternative to merging. Where a merge preserves the full history of both
branches, a rebase replays your commits on top of the latest upstream changes to produce a
cleaner, linear history. For everyday feature branch work, merging is simpler and safer; rebase
is a more advanced technique best explored once you are comfortable with the fundamentals.

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 58
chunks.content:
Chapter 3 58
We will use these git push and git pull commands extensively in our hands-on exercise
later in this chapter. For now, understanding their purpose is key: pushing sends changes out,
and pulling brings changes in.
Now that idx_75c70213 you understand how to commit, push, and pull changes, the next step is learning
how to manage multiple streams of work efficiently. In the following section, we'll explore
branching and the GitFlow strategy, which form the backbone of collaborative development in
Git.
Troubleshooting: Authentication, credentials, and VS Code
Git global configuration: Before your first push, Git needs to know who you are. If you
skipped this step in Chapter 2, run these two commands now; they only need to be set

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
GitHub authentication with HTTPS: When you push to GitHub over HTTPS for the
first time, it will ask for your idx_c37f0884 credentials. GitHub no longer accepts plain passwords;
you must use a Personal Access Token (PAT) instead. Generate one at github.com →
Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens, and use that token
as your password when prompted. To avoid re-entering it every time, enable Git's
credential helper with git config --global credential.helper store (macOS
users can use osxkeychain instead of store).
If code . is not recognized: The code command is installed by VS Code's Shell
Command feature. If your terminal says command not found: code, open VS Code,
press Cmd + Shift + P (macOS) or Ctrl + Shift + P (Windows/Linux), type Shell
Command: Install 'code' command in PATH, and select it. Then restart your
terminal.
Note
59 Mastering Version Control with Git and GitHub
Branching for collaboration: The GitFlow strategy
If committing is how you save idx_fc0f0cc6 your work, branching is how you organize it. A branch in Git is
essentially a idx_1db6641d movable pointer to one of your commits. It represents an independent line of
development. Branching is a core concept that allows you and your team to work on multiple
features, bug fixes, and experiments simultaneously without interfering with each other's
work or destabilizing the main code base. In this section, we'll explore why branching is so
critical and introduce a popular, structured idx_4aa8a977 branching model called GitFlow.
Why do we need branches?
Imagine a team of five developers all working directly on the main version of the code at the
same time. Developer A is working on a complex, half-finished feature. Developer B is trying to
fix an urgent bug. Developer C is refactoring a large part of the application. The code base
would be idx_3ea58a8c in a constant state of flux and instability. It would be impossible to make a clean

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 58
chunks.content:
release because some features would be incomplete and others might be broken.
Branches solve idx_0e2f5164 this problem by providing isolation. The main line of development, typically
idx_72da0983 called the main branch or master branch, is kept clean and idx_a9b67d37 stable at all times. It should
always represent a production-ready version of the software. When a developer wants to start
working on something new, they create a new branch. This new branch is a copy of the main
branch at that point in time. The developer can then work freely on their new branch, making
commits without affecting anyone else. Once their work is complete and tested, they can
merge their branch back into the main branch, integrating their new feature into the official
code base.
Introducing the GitFlow strategy
While you can name and use branches however you like, most successful teams adopt a
standardized idx_cd4df1d8 branching strategy to keep their workflow organized. One of the most popular
and influential strategies is GitFlow, first proposed by Vincent Driessen. GitFlow provides a
robust framework for managing a project with a clear structure for different types of
development work. While some modern, continuous deployment-focused teams have moved
to simpler models, understanding GitFlow is incredibly valuable because it introduces the
concepts behind structured branching.
GitFlow uses two long-lived branches and several types of temporary, supporting branches.
The GitFlow model can be visualized through a branching diagram that shows how the main
(or master) and develop branches interact with feature, release, and hotfix branches:

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 60
chunks.content:
Chapter 3 60
Figure 3.2: The GitFlow model
Let's take a idx_68fab888 closer look at the key branches that form the backbone of this workflow, starting
with the two long-lived branches that define the project's core structure.
Long-lived branches
These branches serve as the permanent foundation of your repository. They represent the most
stable idx_b71cbe4c and critical stages of your code base—the production-ready idx_035e82f6 main branch and the
actively developed integration branch:
master (or main): This branch is the source of truth for your production code. It
should only contain stable, released versions of your software. The code in main is what
your users are currently using. You should never commit directly to this branch.
Commits to main are typically made only when a new version is released and are often
tagged with a version number (e.g., v1.0.1).
develop: This is the primary development branch. It contains the latest delivered
development changes for the next release. You can think of it as the integration branch
for all features. While it should always be in a state where it could potentially be
released, it is where the active work happens. All new feature branches are created from
develop.
While the long-lived branches provide stability, day-to-day development happens on
temporary supporting branches created for specific purposes.
•
•
61 Mastering Version Control with Git and GitHub
Supporting branches
These supporting idx_4cea2f47 branches enable teams to work in parallel, isolate changes, and idx_4a59008b maintain a
clean, controlled flow from feature development to production. Each type of branch has a
distinct role in managing updates, releases, and urgent fixes:
Feature branches (e.g., feature/add-login-page): When you start working on a new
feature, you create a feature branch from the develop branch. This is where you idx_4e1116d2 do all
your development work for that feature. The name of the branch should be descriptive
of its purpose. Once the feature is complete, you merge it back into the develop branch
to await the next release. Feature branches should never interact directly with the main
branch.
Release branches (e.g., release/v1.2.0): When the develop branch has acquired
enough idx_add0d6f4 features for a new release, you create a release branch from develop. The
purpose of this branch is to prepare for a new production release. No new features
should be added to this branch. It is only used for final bug fixes, documentation
generation, and other release-oriented tasks. Once the release branch is stable and
ready, it is merged into both the main branch (to make it the new production version)
and the develop branch (to ensure any bug fixes made in the release branch are also
available for future features). The commit on main is then tagged with the version

chunks.content:
number.
Hotfix branches (e.g., hotfix/fix-critical-bug): A hotfix branch is used to quickly
patch idx_398e7cca a critical bug in the production version. It is the only type of branch that is
created directly from the main branch. You create the branch, fix the bug, and then
merge the hotfix branch back into both main and develop to ensure the fix is included
in the next release as well.
GitFlow provides a clear, disciplined process that separates new development from release
stabilization and production maintenance. It gives teams a shared understanding of how to
manage their code, which is invaluable for collaboration at scale.
Now, it's time to put all this theory into practice.

In this idx_cf1d5b9d section, we will simulate a common workflow: creating a project on GitHub, cloning it
to your machine, creating a feature branch, and pushing it back to GitHub. This exercise will
cement your understanding of the fundamental Git workflow in a collaborative context.
Step 1: Create a new repository on GitHub
First, log in idx_8b57bb99 to your GitHub account. We will create a new, empty repository to host our project.
In the top-right corner of any GitHub page, click the + icon, and then select New

Provide a short description, such as My first collaborative project for the
DevOps book.

initialize the repository with a first commit, which is a common starting point.

Step 3: Create and work on a feature branch
Now, let's follow the GitFlow model. We won't work directly on the main branch. Instead, we'll
idx_847fa953 create a feature branch to work on idx_d88b2b7c a new change. Let's pretend we are adding a basic HTML
page to our project.
First, create and switch to a new feature branch. The git checkout -b <branch-
name> command is a convenient shortcut that does both in one step.
git checkout -b feature/add-homepage
Now you are on your new branch. Let's create a new file. We'll add a simple index.html

Chapter 3 66
Now, push your new branch and its commit to the remote repository on GitHub. The
first time you push a new branch, you need to tell Git to set up a tracking relationship
with the remote branch. The -u flag does this for you.
git push -u origin feature/add-homepage
If you idx_36602b47 now go back to your repository idx_6bdb26a3 page on GitHub and refresh, you will see a message
saying that a new branch was recently pushed, and you'll see your feature/add-homepage
branch listed in the branch dropdown. Your local work is now safely backed up and visible to
your team on GitHub.
You've successfully pushed a feature branch to GitHub. But how do you get that code into the
main branch? You could merge it locally and push main, but that's not how collaborative teams
work. The next step is to open a pull request. Let's learn how.
The power of pull requests and code reviews
A Pull Request (PR) is a formal idx_75aea8f8 proposal to merge your changes from your feature branch into
another branch (usually main or develop). It is the heart of collaboration on GitHub, providing
a dedicated forum for discussing changes, performing code reviews, and running automated
checks before the code is integrated.
Creating your first PR
When you idx_f59b74d1 pushed your feature branch in the last section, GitHub likely displayed a prompt to
create a PR. Let's go through that process now:
On your GitHub repository page, click the Compare & pull request button that
appeared for your feature/add-homepage branch.
It's a common convention to prefix commit messages with a type, such as the
following:
feat: for a new feature
fix: for a bug fix
docs: for documentation changes
This practice, known as conventional commits, makes the project
history much easier to read.

Write a description for your PR. This is your chance to explain why you made these

chunks.content:
Chapter 3 68
Your pull request is now open. This creates a dedicated page where your team can review your
work.
The art of the code review
The code review idx_9ccce767 process is one of the most valuable practices in software development,
offering several key benefits:
Improving code quality: Your teammates might spot bugs, performance issues, or
logical errors that you missed. A second pair of eyes is invaluable.
Sharing knowledge: When a senior developer reviews a junior developer's code, it's a
powerful mentoring opportunity. Conversely, when a junior developer reviews a
senior's code, they can learn new techniques and patterns. It ensures that more than
one person understands every part of the code base.
Maintaining consistency: Code reviews help enforce team-wide coding standards and
architectural patterns, keeping the code base clean and consistent.
Fostering collaboration: PR discussions build a shared sense of ownership and a
collaborative team culture.
A good code idx_4a1d2dea review is a dialogue. As a reviewer, your goal is to be helpful and constructive, not
just to point out flaws. Focus on the "why" behind your suggestions. Instead of just saying
"This is wrong," try "Have you considered this alternative approach? It might be more
performant because..." As the author of the PR, be open to feedback and don't take suggestions
personally. The goal is to collectively create the best possible product.
On the PR page, you can click on the Files changed tab to see a line-by-line view of what was
added, removed, or changed. Reviewers can click on any line to leave a comment. Once the
discussion is complete and everyone is happy with the changes, the PR can be merged.

69 Mastering Version Control with Git and GitHub
Merging the pull request
Once a PR has been approved (and any automated checks have passed), a user with the correct
idx_5175913d permissions can merge it. In professional repositories, the main branch is typically protected, a
GitHub setting found under Settings → Branches → Branch protection rules, that prevents
anyone from pushing directly to main and requires all changes to come through a reviewed PR.
These rules can also mandate that certain CI checks pass before idx_adbf9b35 a merge is allowed. CI
(Continuous Integration) checks are automated pipelines, such as running your test suite or a
code linter, that GitHub triggers automatically each time a PR is updated. You'll see their status
displayed directly on the PR page as green checkmarks or red crosses. We will explore CI
pipelines in depth in a later chapter; for now, understand that they are your safety net before
code ever reaches production. To complete the PR process and merge your changes into the
main branch, follow these steps:
On the PR page, click the green Merge pull request button.

You will be asked to confirm the merge. You can edit the default commit message if you
wish.
Click Confirm merge.
The code from your feature/add-homepage branch is now officially part of the main branch.
GitHub will also give you the option to delete the feature branch, which is a good practice to
keep the repository clean. Congratulations, you have just completed a full, collaborative
workflow using a pull request!
As you and idx_f360a8ab your team work on a project, you will inevitably encounter a merge conflict. This
sounds intimidating, but it's a normal and manageable part of working with Git. Let's learn
how to resolve them.
Resolving merge conflicts
A merge conflict occurs when idx_3917dd13 two developers make conflicting idx_ff5c9814 changes to the same lines in
the same file on different branches. When you try to merge these branches, Git doesn't know
which change is correct, so it stops and asks you, the human, to resolve the ambiguity.
How does a merge conflict happen?
Let's imagine a simple scenario:
You and idx_8cd62c4b your colleague, Jane, both start with the same version of the README.md file,
which contains the line Welcome to our project.
You create a branch called feature/update-readme-A and change that line to Welcome
to our awesome project. You commit and push your branch.

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 70
chunks.content:
Chapter 3 70
At the same time, Jane creates a branch called feature/update-readme-B and changes
the same line to Welcome to our new project. She commits and pushes her branch.
Jane creates a pull request first, and it gets merged into main. The main branch now
contains her change.
Now, you create a PR to merge your branch into main. Git sees that the line you changed
has also been changed on the main branch since you created your branch. It cannot
automatically decide which version is correct. This is a merge conflict.
How to resolve a conflict
When a idx_2dc1741b conflict occurs, GitHub will prevent you from merging the PR and will show a message
that says This branch has conflicts that must be resolved. You must resolve the conflict
locally on your machine before you can complete the merge.
First, make sure your local main branch is up to date with the remote repository:
git checkout main
git pull origin main
Now, switch back to your feature branch:
git checkout feature/update-readme-A
Try to merge the main branch into your feature branch. This will bring the conflict
onto your local machine, where you can fix it:
git merge main
Git will fail idx_8e348505 and give you a message such as CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in
README.md.
Open the conflicted file (README.md) in VS Code. Git will have modified the file to show
you exactly where the conflict is. It will look something like this:

chunks.title: clouddevopsengineersguide
chunks.heading: <<<<<<< HEAD
chunks.content:
<<<<<<< HEAD
Welcome to our awesome project.
=======
Welcome to our new project.
>>>>>>> main

chunks.heading: 4.71 Mastering Version Control with Git and GitHub
chunks.sectionTitle: Mastering Version Control with Git and GitHub
chunks.content:
4.71 Mastering Version Control with Git and GitHub
Git is showing you both versions of the line. The code between < < < < < < < HEAD
and ======= is your change from your current branch (HEAD). The code between
======= and > > > > > > > main is the change coming from the main branch.
To resolve the conflict, you must manually edit the file to be exactly how you want it to
end up. You need to delete the conflict markers (< < < < < < <, =======, > > > > > >
>) and choose which version to keep, or even write a completely new version that
combines both. For example, you might decide the best version is Welcome to our
new, awesome project..
After you have edited the file and saved it, you need to tell Git that you have resolved
the conflict. You do this by staging the file:
git add README.md
Now, complete the merge by making a new commit:
git commit
Git will create a default commit message for you, which you can usually keep.
Finally, push your updated feature branch (which now contains both your changes and
the merge conflict resolution) back to GitHub.
git push origin feature/update-readme-A
If you go back idx_ffb2f545 to your pull request on GitHub, you will see that the conflict warning is gone,
and the PR is now ready to be merged. Handling merge conflicts is a vital skill, and while it can
be stressful at first, it becomes a routine part of the development process.
5.
VS Code to the rescue
VS Code has excellent tools for resolving conflicts. It will highlight the
conflicting blocks and often provide clickable links to Accept Current Change,
Accept Incoming Change, or Accept Both Changes, which can speed up the
process significantly.
